# A test's trigger evaluates its argument once on every target. The
# interpreter evaluated a one-argument trigger's arguments to ask whether the
# event presses a copy of a loop (a tab of a strip), and again to fire it when
# it does not, so `c.pick.change(next())` ran `next` twice there and once on
# every compiled target. And android's test spelled the argument with no
# receiver, so `next`, a function of the page the state class holds, was an
# unresolved reference; it is read as an assertion reads its expression.

sngl test --platform=none app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'
sngl test --platform=html app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'
sngl test --platform=bubbletea --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'
sngl test --platform=fyne --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'
sngl test --platform=gtk4 --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'
sngl test --platform=android --language=kotlin app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'

-- app.sngl --
import test "sngl:test"
import ui "sngl:ui"

var asked = 0

func next() string {
    asked += 1
    return "b"
}

component page ui.node {
    var picked = "a"

    ui.select #pick(:value=picked) {
        ui.choice(label="a")
        ui.choice(label="b")
    }
}

func testATriggersArgumentRunsOnce(t test.Test, c page) {
    c.pick.change(next())
    t.assert(c.picked == "b")
    t.assert(asked == 1)
}

ui.window {
    page()
}
